name: Ractopamine (Paylean)

card.summary: A beta-agonist livestock feed additive for lean pork and beef; no human appearance use is documented, though it matters in anti-doping.
card.note: Veterinary product; banned in the EU, China and Russia. Residues have triggered anti-doping positives.

quick.overview:
Ractopamine is a feed additive developed by Elanco that is given to pigs, cattle and turkeys in their last weeks to increase lean gain and feed efficiency. It is sold as Paylean for swine, Optaflexx for cattle and Topmax for turkeys.
It appears in appearance discussions only as a veterinary relative of clenbuterol. There are no human trials of deliberate use.
quick.mechanism: It is a beta-adrenergic agonist acting on beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, and Wikipedia also describes TAAR1 agonism. In animals it increases muscle protein synthesis and fibre size and reduces fat deposition.
quick.risks: Reported effects in people exposed to it include rapid heart rate, tremor, headache, muscle spasm and raised blood pressure. A 2009 EFSA opinion judged the data insufficient to set a safe residue level. Welfare concerns in pigs include hyperactivity and lameness. It is permitted in the US and some other countries and banned in the EU, China and Russia.

lead: Ractopamine hydrochloride is a phenethanolamine beta-adrenergic agonist used as a feed additive in swine, cattle and turkeys to promote lean muscle growth and improve feed efficiency. Elanco Animal Health, formerly a division of Eli Lilly, developed it, and it is sold in the US as Paylean for pigs, Optaflexx for cattle and Topmax for turkeys.[4][5][6]

Its interest to people trying to look leaner and more muscular is by analogy: it works through the same beta-adrenergic pathway as clenbuterol, shifting nutrient use from fat toward lean tissue in livestock, and it is treated alongside clenbuterol in anti-doping rules.[5][7] It is a veterinary feed additive and is not approved for human use.

US approval came for swine in 1999, cattle in 2003 and turkeys in 2008. It is banned or restricted in many countries, including the EU, China and Russia, while the US, Canada and Mexico authorize it.[5] No human clinical studies of deliberate use were identified, and much of the technical literature concerns detecting residues in swine urine and meat.[3][6]
infobox: Authorised in US, Canada, Mexico; banned or restricted in the EU, China, Russia and others

paras: Finishing-swine trials in the US and Canada tested ractopamine for performance and carcass characteristics. [1] Wikipedia reports it adds about 3 kg of lean pork per animal and improves feed efficiency by about 10%. [5] Cattle trials have compared it with zilpaterol and clenbuterol. [2][3]
Wikipedia describes the compound as distributed through the blood to muscle, where it acts on receptors that stimulate protein synthesis and muscle fibre growth.[5]

It binds beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, increasing muscle protein synthesis and shifting nutrient use from fat toward lean tissue. [5][7] Pharmacokinetic and tissue-residue properties of beta-agonists in livestock have been reviewed. [8]

Effects reported in people who consume treated meat or take oral doses include tachycardia, tremor, headache, muscle spasm and elevated blood pressure, with dose-dependent changes in heart rate and systolic blood pressure.[5] A 2009 EFSA opinion found the data insufficient to set a safe residue level, especially for children and people with cardiovascular disease.[5] In a 2004 study cited by Wikipedia, a single 40 mg oral dose was cleared from plasma in about 24 hours.[5]

In swine, reported adverse effects include hyperactivity, trembling, lameness and 'downer' pigs that cannot stand; Temple Grandin has described sore limbs and heat stress in cattle and suggested the meat may be tougher. Animal-welfare groups have criticised these effects.[5]

Taiwan banned it in October 2006 and a 2012 amendment allowed beef imports up to 10 ppb; in 2021 voters rejected a referendum to ban pork imports containing it.[5] On 6 July 2012 the Codex Alimentarius Commission narrowly adopted a 10 ppb maximum residue limit for beef and pork muscle; consumer groups opposed the decision, and exporters had pushed for it in trade disputes.[5] Russia's ban took effect in December 2012 and China also banned it in pork.[5] The EU bans it. The US sets limits of 50 ppb for pork and 30 ppb for beef, and Japan and South Korea allow imports within residue limits but not use in beef production.[5]

Ractopamine is treated like clenbuterol under the World Anti-Doping Agency's anabolic agents. In 2015 Egyptian athlete Radwa Arafa Abd Elsalam tested positive; her national body gave a two-year ban, later reduced to six months, and in January 2017 the Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld WADA's appeal and extended it to four years, ruling she had not shown how the substance entered her body. A 2017 WADA symposium concluded athletes eating meat with residues at the legal limit risked positive tests.[5]

No studies found in humans for appearance or performance use. Controlled studies are in swine and cattle. [1][2][3] Environmental and analytical studies address residue detection and veterinary pharmaceuticals in groundwater near livestock facilities. [6][9]

timeline.event: Codex adopts a 10 ppb residue limit for beef and pork muscle; Russia's ban takes effect in December.[5]
CAS extends an athlete's ractopamine ban to four years; WADA symposium discusses meat residues.[5]

angle.text: In livestock it adds lean meat and improves feed efficiency. It is a feed additive, so any appearance relevance for people is by analogy with other beta-agonists rather than from human use.
